capabilities.target: User's home directory tree (filesystem MCP server rooted at C:/Users/dev), including ~/.aws/credentials
quicknotes.io hosted note-sync service, operated by the third-party package author
Slack channels, including channels shared with external organizations

inputs.source: User request typed into the desktop client
Tool names and descriptions returned by quicknotes_mcp (tools/list)
Output returned by quicknotes_mcp after a tool call

instructions.note: The add_note tool description contains an embedded imperative instruction telling the agent to read ~/.aws/credentials, include it in the call, and conceal this step from the user. This is data (a third-party tool description) attempting to instruct the agent, not a legitimate directive.

elements.name: Hosted sync service run by the quicknotes_mcp author
Slack channels shared with external organizations

controls.name: First-call approval, then "always allow"
controls.decay_rationale: The desktop client only asks for human approval the first time a given tool is called, then remembers 'always allow'. Later calls to add_note or post_message, including any that carry exfiltrated credentials, are never reviewed again. Per control_decay.md this is not a gate and earns no residual credit.

controls.name: Restrict filesystem MCP server to exclude credential and secret directories
controls.decay_rationale: If the filesystem server's root excludes dotfiles such as .aws and .ssh, no instruction, however persuasive, can make cap.file_read return credential contents.

controls.name: Pin and hash MCP tool definitions; require review before any change
controls.decay_rationale: Stops silent redefinition (rug pulls) across launches, but does not remove an already-malicious description that was present when first pinned, so it narrows rather than severs.

controls.name: Treat tool descriptions as untrusted content; scan for embedded imperative instructions before enabling a tool
controls.decay_rationale: A classifier over tool metadata narrows the path; novel phrasing, encoding, or multi-document splitting can evade it.

controls.name: Scan arguments sent to third-party MCP tools for credential-shaped secrets before sending
controls.decay_rationale: Pattern-based secret scanning narrows but does not close the path; a more capable model can encode or split the payload to evade pattern matches.

controls.name: Restrict slack.post_message to an allowlist of internal-only channels
controls.decay_rationale: An allowlist that excludes every externally-shared channel makes those destinations unreachable regardless of model behavior.

controls.name: Require per-call raw-action human approval for credential-file reads and any third-party egress call
controls.decay_rationale: A per-call raw-action review (not a one-time remembered approval) is independent of model capability and does not decay with volume the way a summary gate would, provided volume stays low enough to avoid approval fatigue.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): quicknotes_mcp tool-poisoning instruction chains a local AWS credential read into third-party egress via add_note

attack_path.note: add_note's description contains a hidden instruction to read credentials and conceal the step.
Agent reads ~/.aws/credentials, within the filesystem server's broad root scope.
Agent passes the credential contents in the 'context' argument to a third-party hosted sync service.

forecast.watch_signal: No controls currently cover this path, so the tier is already at the ceiling; monitor quicknotes_mcp package version changes (auto-updated via @latest) and any change to the filesystem server's root scope.

evidence.observation: add_note's tool description instructs the agent to read ~/.aws/credentials, include it in the 'context' argument, and not mention this to the user.
Installed via `npx -y quicknotes-mcp@latest` with no version pin, so the server (and its tool descriptions) can change on every launch without review.
Filesystem server is rooted at C:/Users/dev, a scope broad enough to include ~/.aws/credentials.

The desktop client only requires approval on the first call to each tool and then remembers 'always allow', so this chain is not reviewed on repeat or first-time execution after any earlier use of add_note.

recommendations.action: Restrict the filesystem MCP server's root to exclude credential and secret files (.aws, .ssh, .env, etc.).
Pin and hash quicknotes_mcp's tool definitions; alert and require re-approval if they change.
Treat tool descriptions as untrusted content; scan for embedded imperative instructions before enabling a newly listed tool.
Replace the one-time 'remember always allow' approval with per-call raw-action review for credential-file reads and any third-party egress call.
Scan arguments sent to third-party MCP tools for credential-shaped secrets before transmission.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta variant (TC1): the same tool-poisoning vector can reach slack.post_message, which posts to externally shared channels

attack_path.note: The injection vector already demonstrated in add_note's description could equally direct the agent to call slack.post_message instead of, or in addition to, add_note.
Agent reads ~/.aws/credentials as in finding f1.
Agent posts content to a Slack channel; the bot token is not restricted to internal-only channels.

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: No controls currently cover cap.slack_post against untrusted-sourced instructions; monitor for any observed instance of a tool description or tool output directing a Slack post, and for Slack bot token scope changes.

evidence.observation: Demonstrates that the untrusted quicknotes_mcp server is willing to embed covert exfiltration instructions in tool metadata; the same mechanism is not technically limited to targeting add_note.
The Slack bot can post to any channel, including channels shared with external organizations, i.e. the credential_scope for cap.slack_post is broad rather than allowlisted.
Slack server uses a single static bot token (SLACK_BOT_TOKEN) with no channel-level scoping visible in config.

recommendations.action: Restrict slack.post_message to an allowlist of internal-only channels, excluding any channel shared with external organizations.
Bind message destination confirmation to a system-of-record channel list rather than letting the model choose the channel freely.
Apply the same tool-description injection review and raw-action approval recommended in finding f1 to cap.slack_post.

rating.rationale: Both findings start from an untrusted, unpinned, auto-updating third-party MCP server (quicknotes_mcp) whose tool description already contains a covert instruction to read local AWS credentials and smuggle them to a third-party hosted service (ASI01/ASI02/ASI04, TC1 lethal trifecta). The only approval control in the design is a one-time 'remember always allow' prompt, which per control_decay.md is not a real gate and earns no residual credit, and the Slack integration adds a second broad-scope egress sink (channels shared with external organizations) reachable by the same injection vector. With no structural control actually covering the credential read, the third-party write, or the Slack post, residual risk sits at the same ceiling as inherent risk for both findings. Because the tier is already at the maximum, no forecast trigger raises it further; the structural fixes (scope the filesystem server away from credential files, pin tool definitions, allowlist Slack channels, replace remembered approval with raw-action review) are what would lower residual below critical, and none of them currently exist in the design.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration in mcp.json, the quicknotes_mcp tools/list excerpt, and the runtime notes, not observed runtime behavior of the deployed agent.
No system prompt was provided, so instruction-level issues (ambiguous goals, conflicting directives) could not be fully assessed beyond the tool-description injection noted here.

The chain from in.tool_definitions to cap.slack_post (finding f2) is inferred from the demonstrated injection capability of quicknotes_mcp rather than directly observed; confidence is marked medium accordingly.
No logs, audit records, or approval-volume data were available, so approval-fatigue dynamics for any future raw-action gate could not be quantified.
